name: Abdul Samad Zeeshan
role: Backend and data systems, some with a model inside
intro: I finished my Computing Science degree at the University of Alberta in June 2026. I build backend services, data pipelines and systems with a language model somewhere inside. Every project below solves one real problem, and its page shows what actually happened when I tested it.

edges.evidence: The agent, the server it calls and the risk scoring are written in Python. The results tables are rebuilt from saved files.
A LangGraph agent gathers the facts on each change, but it never has the power to approve anything alone.
The agent reaches its tools through a Model Context Protocol server. Over that link, none of 84 attacks got through.
Tools arrive only when a step needs them, and the power to write arrives only after the risk is scored.
Each credential is short-lived and names one customer and one request. Seven ways of forging one got zero calls served.
The same defences held against a real login server and Postgres database. None of 84 attacks got through there either.
The approval rules live in one versioned file. A solver checks each new version against the last one before it counts.
A test fails if any results table in the write-up drifts from the saved result files.
The fake customers, the recorder between agent and tools, and the report are Python, with automated tests.
It tests an AI agent on made-up customers, with its tools recorded or faked so nothing real is touched.
Hostile fake customers pushed the old Warden into 1.3 unwanted server calls per conversation. The new version made 0.6, so it shipped.
Three automatic judges were tuned on known answers, then checked against what really happened on 240 sampled calls.
A run recorded with a local model replays in automated tests with no model at all.
The service is plain Java on the built-in web server, with lightweight threads and hand-written JSON.
Database rules back the ledger rules. Each payment key is unique, ordinary balances cannot go below zero, and no entry is zero.
A payment retried after a lost reply lands exactly once. None of about 1,600 retries was applied twice.
Account rows are locked in one fixed order, so two crossing transfers can never block each other forever.
A TLA+ model follows the transfer code line by line. It passed across about 390,000 distinct states.
Transfers kept flowing while the network and database were made to fail. Over about 11,000 transfers, not one cent was lost or doubled.
It is deployed to a local Kubernetes cluster from plain config files, and must pass four release checks plus a failure check.
Of transfers flagged as fraud on new data, 82% really were fraud. The first rules managed 37%.
A checker rebuilt 16 fraud signals for all 9,290 payments using only earlier data. It found no mismatches.
Metrics are hand-written, and speed is timed from when each request was meant to go out, so waiting in line counts.
A small, fixed web API sits over the ledger, with no framework.
Automated checks rerun the failure tests on every push as the fifth release check.
The conversation logic, the booking service and the tests are Python, and the tests need no models.
Speech works on one laptop with no internet. Only 17 of 40 scripted calls ended in a booking, which is not good enough yet.
When the booking system failed mid-call, Parley handled it safely all 232 times and never spoke a false fact.
The same scripted calls are replayed with clean audio, noisy audio, garbled text and a failing booking system.
The booking system is made slow, empty, contradictory or down mid-call, and Parley books a callback instead of guessing.
Automated checks fail if the tables in the write-up drift from the results file.
The detector, the checker and the scoring are Python, reading a local copy of the full login log.
Batch and live scoring share one Spark code path over the full log of about a billion events.
The first version keeps a dbt and DuckDB warehouse over the stored logins.
Each login is scored as it arrives, and logins in the same second never see each other.
The first version keeps a Neo4j graph of which user logged into which computer.
Detector inputs were recomputed with the future hidden, about 5.1 million of them. None changed, so nothing peeked ahead.
At 100 alerts a day, it caught attacker activity on 29 of 181 days. The first rules caught 21. Most still got through.
Every detector learns only from the first day and is scored against the lab's answer key, bad results included.
An AI analyst asks questions about the login map through a fixed list of tools. Made-up tool calls are refused.
The analyst's confidence was close to its real hit rate, off by 0.04 with map tools and 0.05 without. Only 49 alerts were scored.
Automated checks run the same code on a small saved slice of the log and fail if the tables drift.
The training and scoring code is Python.
After fine-tuning, the small model gave 87.2% of unseen support emails the right urgency. Before training it managed 38.3%.
A large hosted model labels the emails, and the small model learns to copy those labels.
It returns topic, urgency and account number as clean JSON, offline, with no outside service.
It sorted 90.0% of the same 1,200 emails into the right topic. Before training it managed 64.2%.
The pipeline, its tests and its scoring are TypeScript.
It is built on AWS storage, queues, functions and a database. It was deployed to a test account, checked, then torn down.
When the model was forced to follow the output format, all 20 photo receipts came back as valid JSON. Without that, 17 of 20.
Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock got almost every field right on 42 hand-checked receipts, scoring 0.999, from saved answers.
Some test receipts were trusted to skip a person, 11 of 149 at a 1% error budget. None of their 32 fields were wrong.
Each record's id comes from the file itself, so a repeated delivery never makes a second record.
Alarms went quiet after a security setting silently removed their right to publish. The alarm topic now grants it in writing.
